questions.question: subtract one from any positive number of positive numbers on the board. The game ends once all numbers are 0, and the last player who made a move wins. If Lizzie always plays first, find all n for which Lizzie has a winning strategy. 4/3/35. In this problem, a simple polygon is a polygon that does not intersect itself and has no holes, and a side of a polygon is a maximal set of collinear, consecutive line segments in the polygon. In particular, we allow two or more consecutive vertices in a simple polygon to be identical, and three or more consecutive vertices in a simple polygon to be collinear. By convention, polygons must have at least three sides. A simple polygon is convex if every one of its interior angles is 180 ◦ or less. A simple polygon is concave if it is not convex. Let P be the plane. Prove or disprove each of the following statements: (a) There exists a function f : P → P such that for all positive integers n ≥ 4, if v1, v 2, . . . , v n are the vertices of a simple concave n-sided polygon in some order, then f(v1), f (v2), . . . , f (vn) are the vertices of a simple convex polygon in some order (which may or may not have n sides). (b) There exists a function f : P → P such that for all positive integers n ≥ 4, if v1, v 2, . . . , v n are the vertices of a simple convex n-sided polygon in some order, then f(v1), f (v2), . . . , f (vn) are the vertices of a simple concave polygon in some order (which may or may not have n sides). 5/3/35. Let ω be the unit circle in the xy-plane in 3-dimensional space. Find all points P not on the xy-plane that satisfy the following condition: There exist points A, B, and C on ω such that ∠AP B = ∠AP C = ∠BP C = 90◦. Problems by USAMTS Staff. questions.solution: Subtracting one from any positive number of positive numbers on the board means we can either take any number of steps south (in the case where we subtracting one from ones only), or we can move northwest any number of steps (in the case where we are subtracting one from twos only, effectively exchanging twos for ones), or we can move along some combination of first south, then northwest (removing ones and exchanging twos for ones simultaneously). Note that the order matters here: we cannot go northwest and then south, since that would require two moves (first, exchanging twos for ones, and second, removing those newly acquired ones) From these interpretations, we can see that every point of the form (0 , y) with y > 0 is hot, and the point (1 , 0) is also hot: Number of twos Number of ones Then the point (1 , 1) is cold, since everywhere it reaches in one move is hot: Create PDF with GO2PDF for free, if you wish to remove this line, click here to buy Virtual PDF Printer USA Mathematical Talent Search Round 3 Solutions Year 35 — Academic Year 2023–2024 www.usamts.org Number of twos Number of ones The locus of points that can reach the cold point (1 , 1) is then all the remaining uncate- gorized points on the line x = 1 as well as all the points on the line x = 2. Number of twos Number of ones Then, the point (3 , 0) will be cold, since it can only reach hot positions in one move: Create PDF with GO2PDF for free, if you wish to remove this line, click here to buy Virtual PDF Printer USA Mathematical Talent Search Round 3 Solutions Year 35 — Academic Year 2023–2024 www.usamts.org Number of twos Number of ones At this point, due to the geometry of the moves, the entire pattern will continue to repeat in cycles of 3 columns. So the grid will be colored as follows: Number of twos Number of ones ... ... We see that when y = 0, the x for which Lizzie has a winning strategy for are x = 1, 2, 4, 5, . . . , that is, the values of x that are of the form 3k + 1 or 3k + 2 . The overall winning strategy is to always make moves that leave Alex with a position of the form (3 j, 0) or (3j + 1, 1). Let ω be the unit circle in the xy-plane in 3-dimensional space. Find all points P not on the xy-plane that satisfy the following condition: There exist points A, B, and C on ω such that ∠AP B = ∠AP C = ∠BP C = 90◦. Solution Let A, B, C, and P be points that satisfy the given conditions. Let D be the projection of A onto BC. Let O2 be the midpoint of AC, and let O3 be the midpoint of AB. Then D is the reflection of A in O2O3. Since ∠AP B = 90◦, P lies on the sphere centered at O3 with radius AB 2 . Also, ∠ADB = 90◦, so D also lies on this sphere. Likewise, P and D lie on the sphere centered at O2 with radius AC 2 . The intersection of these two spheres is a circle that contains A, P , and D. Also, the plane of this circle is perpendicular to O2O3. Since BC is parallel to O2O3, plane AP D is also perpendicular to BC. It follows that P D is perpendicular to BC. Let H be the projection of P onto plane ABC. Then P H is perpendicular to BC. Both P D and P H are perpendicular to BC, so plane P HD is perpendicular to BC. But AD is perpendicular to BC, so plane P HD contains point A. Furthermore, points D and H lie in plane ABC, so H lies on altitude AD. Similarly, H lies on altitudes BE and CF of triangle ABC, so H is the orthocenter of triangle ABC. Let ABC be a triangle with circumcenter O, A-excenter IA, B-excenter IB, and C- excenter IC. The incircle of ∆ABC is tangent to sides BC, CA, and AB at D, E, and F respectively. Lines IBE and ICF intersect at P. If the line through O perpendicular to OP passes through IA, prove that ∠A = 60◦. An excenter is the point of concurrency among one internal angle bisector and two ex- ternal angle bisectors of a triangle. Solution A BCD E FI OOe IA IB IC P Let Oe be the circumcenter of ∆IAIBIC. EF and IBIC are both perpendicular to the internal angle bisector AIA of ∠BAC, so EF‖ IBIC. Similarly, F D‖ ICIA and DE‖ IAIB. Thus,∆DEF and∆IAIBIC are homothetic. The center of homothety is IBE∩ ICF = P. The homothety centered at P carrying∆DEF to∆IAIBIC must also carry the circum- center I of∆DEF to the circumcenter Oe of∆IAIBIC, so P is collinear with I and Oe. I is the incenter of ∆ABC, so it is also the orthocenter of ∆IAIBIC. Therefore P IOe is the Euler line of∆IAIBIC. Since O is the nine-point center of∆IAIBIC, we know that O lies on the Euler line as well. Thus, OP is actually just the Euler line of ∆IAIBIC. The problem statement gives us that IAO is perpendicular to the Euler line IO e of ∆IAIBIC. However, O is equidistant from I and Oe, so IAO must be the perpendicular bisector of IO e. So IAOe = IAI = 2IO e cos ∠IBIAIC, which occurs only when∠IBIAIC = 60◦. Then ∠A = ∠BAC = 180◦− 2∠IBIAIC = 60◦ as desired.
